title: The key to the workshop
text: The key had been lying at the bottom of an old biscuit tin for as long as Misha could remember, but it was only after his grandfather's funeral that anyone paid it any attention. His mother found it while sorting through papers, and handed it to him without a word. It was small, heavy and slightly warm from her hand. 'The workshop,' she said finally. 'He always said it would be yours one day, if you wanted it.' Misha felt a **lump in his throat** and nodded, because he could not speak.

The workshop was at the end of a narrow courtyard, behind a door that had not been painted for twenty years. Inside, the air smelled of oil, dust and old wood. Clocks hung on every wall, and none of them agreed about the time. Misha, who had been in this room only as a small child, stood still for a while, surprised by how little had changed, and by how much smaller everything seemed. On a shelf above the door stood a row of tins labelled in his grandfather's neat handwriting, each one full of tiny screws sorted by size.

On the workbench, under a green lamp, he found a half-finished clock. Its case was beautifully carved, but the mechanism lay in pieces, each part laid out on a cloth in a careful row, as if the owner had only stepped out for a moment. Beside it was a sheet of paper in his grandfather's shaky handwriting: 'For Misha's eighteenth birthday. Needs a new spring. Be patient.' It dawned on him that the old man had known exactly how little time he had left.

For the next few weeks Misha came every afternoon after school. He had to learn the whole craft from scratch, with only a few books and the occasional visit from the neighbour, a retired engineer named Mr Orlov, who gave advice but refused to touch anything. Springs snapped, screws vanished between the floorboards, and more than once Misha was ready to throw the whole thing into a drawer and forget the workshop altogether. His friends thought he had lost his mind, and Katya, who sat next to him in class, asked him twice whether he was ill, since he had stopped coming to the café.

Mr Orlov's patience was the only thing that never ran out. 'A clock is not a problem to be solved,' he said once, watching Misha curse at a tiny wheel. 'It is a conversation. You must listen to what the parts want.' Misha did not understand, but a week later, as he fitted a spring that finally held, he thought that perhaps he did. The wheel turned, hesitated, and began to tick. He stood very still, afraid that even a breath might spoil it.

On the evening of his birthday the clock stood on the kitchen table, running two minutes slow. His mother looked at it for a long time, and then, to his surprise, she laughed. 'He was always two minutes late for everything,' she said. Misha adjusted nothing. He decided that the clock was keeping exactly the right time, his grandfather's, and that it could go on doing so for as long as it liked. The next morning he would carry it to the neighbour's flat, to show it to the one person who would understand it better than anyone else.

questions.q: Why did Misha's mother give him the key?
options: She wanted him to sell the workshop.
She was too sad to go there herself.
He had asked her for it.

questions.q: What does 'It' in 'It is a conversation' refer to?
'A lump in his throat' in paragraph 1 means that Misha felt …
What did the note on the workbench show?
options: Grandfather wanted Misha to sell the clock.
The old man did not expect to finish the work.

questions.q: What was Mr Orlov's role in the story?
options: He repaired the clock for Misha.
He guided Misha without doing the work.

questions.q: Which of these is NOT mentioned in the text?
options: Misha's friends came to help him.
The finished clock was a little slow.

questions.q: How does Misha feel about the clock at the end?
options: Glad that it recalls his grandfather.
Keen to sell it as soon as possible.
Angry with his mother for laughing.

discuss: Do you have a hobby that someone in your family taught you?
Grandfather said very little but taught a lot. Have you learnt anything from a person who spoke little?
Is it better to follow a family tradition or to choose your own path?
